I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

Launching our leaderboard for FrontierPhysics, including 54 physics research tasks written by physicists. Claude Fable 5.2 leads at 32%, 6 points ahead of GPT-6.2 Astra

FrontierPhysics is a physics research benchmark from 
@benchflow_ai
, and we run 54 of the 56 tasks (excluding two GPU tasks). Each task is written by physicists and requires the agent to review the literature, run simulations and analyses, and submit its results with a manuscript. Tasks span 9 physics domains, from condensed matter to astrophysics, and are private to avoid contamination.

A run passes only if its results pass the task's numeric checks and LLM agent reviewers find no flaw that would prevent publication. A failed run scores 0, and a passing run scores the share of rubric points the reviewers award.

Key takeaways:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 (max) leads by 6 points, and the next five models score between 22% and 26%: GPT-6.2 Astra (max) 26%, Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh) 25%, Claude Opus 5.5 (max) 24%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) 23% and GPT-6.2 Sol (max) 22%

➤ Nearly half of Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh)'s runs that pass the numeric checks fail review: Neon passes numeric checks 54% of the time, the most of any model, but only passes review 28% of the time. The rest have a flaw that would prevent publication, such as an invalid simulation setup, a missing derivation or a written conclusion the results don't support

➤ GPT-6.2 Sol (max) and GPT-6.2 Astra (max) sit on the Pareto frontier for score vs. cost: they score 22% at $1.70 per task and 26% at $5.97. Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh) and Claude Opus 5.5 (max) score within 3 points of GPT-6.2 Astra (max) at $13.69 and $21.93

Announcing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1: frontier language models driving our Unitree G1 humanoid

AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the next one: LLMs in native harnesses directly controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid, with a simple objective for each task. We plan to expand from here.

AA-Robotics-Sim details:

➤ 10 tasks in four groups of skills: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly, tool use, and mobility

➤ For each task, a model first plays five practice episodes to learn the environment and take notes. It’s then evaluated on ten new scenes

➤ Every evaluation scene changes the room, the lighting, the layout, the props, and the details of the task

➤ Each episode is scored 0 to 100 from the simulator's measurements, with partial credit

Key results:

➤ GPT-6.2 Astra leads with 71.0, 13.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 (57.5) and GPT-6.2 Sol (53.7), followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (48.2), Gemini 4 Neon (46.2), GPT-6 Astra (46.1), Gemini 4 Argon (45.5), GPT-6.1 Sol (33.1) and Claude Fable 5.1 (29.1)

➤ Some skills are mature; others are missing from every model: every model walked to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, but only five dishes ended up in the dishwasher rack in 90 episodes

➤ An evaluation episode takes 17 to 39 minutes and costs $0.84 to $9.01, yet the robot moves for under a minute of it

Octen Search (fast, dynamic) returns each search in ~0.17s, the fastest of the 25 Search API products we benchmark, and scores 82 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index

We benchmarked the fast, dynamic mode of 
@OctenAI
's Search API in our Stirrup agent harness with Octen Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

In our September run, Octen Search (highlights) scored 77. In these November runs, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) scores 82.

Key benchmarking results for Octen Search:

➤ Speed: each search returns in about 0.17s, the lowest of the 25 Search API products and about half the next lowest (0.33s). Time per Task is 13.3s, the lowest of 26 and comparable to Parallel Search (fast, objective) (14.3s) and Keenable Search (realtime) (14.4s), against a board median of about 26s

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: 82, 3rd of 26, within 1 point of Parallel Search (advanced, objective) and Keenable Search (pro) at 83. That is a ~49-point lift over the same model with no search (33). No product scores higher in less time

➤ BrowseComp: Octen scores 92% on our hard BrowseComp subset (200 questions), the highest of 26 and ~4 points above Keenable Search (pro) and Perplexity Search (medium) at 87%. Octen scores 84 F1 on DeepSearchQA (7th) and 72% on AA-Omniscience (joint 6th)

➤ Low cost: about $0.018 per task, 3rd lowest of 26 behind TinyFish ($0.009) and Parallel Search (fast, objective) ($0.014), against a board median of $0.063

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Octen Search API with result_type=dynamic

➤ Dynamic results: Octen returns only the results it finds relevant, up to the 10 we request, and sets the highlight length for each result

➤ Pricing: $1 per 1k requests

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

There are a handful of tech right people who have a modicum of situational awareness with respect to ai safety, and it’s not that much of an exaggeration to say that they all work at, or are otherwise affiliated with, 
@JoinFAI

i'm now pretty convinced that one of the most important metrics to watch out for in your codebases when most work is done by agents is -

median $ cost per task

this screenshot is one of my recent codebases which grew from 100k to 1M lines of code over the past month from intense development

the median $ cost of a task kept growing as well. and each time i noticed it was rising, i did some analysis to understand why, and did optimizations to drive it back down

my task cost is actually pretty high because the repo is a cross-platform app and most features need to work on mac, linux, windows, and mobile

i'm reasonably happy that the cost only rose by 70% when the codebase is now 10x complexity. it wouldn't have been possible without lots of optimizations, because agents by default don't care about long term maintainability (explained in a previous tweet)

if i had left it unchecked, every task would have become a lot slower and more costly, and i wouldn't have been able to keep the pace of development

a prompt you can use to start understanding what's happening with your work -

"look at my past month's agent sessions' usage stats in this codebase to calculate a 7d sliding window median $ cost per task and report it as a chart"
